items.prompt: In this unit, what does depth mean?
choices: Reasoning through a domain yourself and verifying claims without help
Knowing which team owns a domain and its common vocabulary
Having sat in many meetings about the domain over the years
items.explanation: Depth means you can verify a claim yourself; knowing owners and vocabulary is breadth.

items.prompt: What is borrowed judgment?
choices: Copying an expert's verdict because they hold a higher title
Acting on an expert's reasoning while still checking it holds together
Asking several people until someone agrees with you
items.explanation: Borrowed judgment uses the expert's reasoning but keeps a check on it.

items.prompt: A doctor nods along to a specialist's jargon and guesses a diagnosis. Which failure mode is this?
choices: Over-investigating: spending effort the case never needed
Delegating: handing the case to the right person
Bluffing: borrowed confidence with no borrowed judgment behind it
items.explanation: Guessing at a diagnosis she does not understand is faking depth.

items.prompt: A doctor orders every possible test for a mild three-day cough. Which failure mode is this?
choices: Bluffing about a skill she does not have at all
Over-investigating a low-stakes call
Breadth used well, exactly as it is intended to be
items.explanation: Heavy effort on a low-risk, reversible call is the over-investigating mode.

items.prompt: Why is breadth the default for most calls?
choices: Depth stops being useful once a role becomes broad
Experts dislike being asked questions by outsiders
Nobody can go deep on every domain a role touches
items.explanation: A broad role makes personal depth everywhere impossible, so breadth must be the default.

items.prompt: Who counts as the domain expert?
choices: Whoever has real depth in the specific mechanism, whatever their title
The highest-ranking person on the team that owns it, since rank signals knowledge
Whoever replies first
items.explanation: Expertise is depth in the specific mechanism, not rank or speed.

items.prompt: Which pair of failure modes does the unit name?
choices: Asking too many experts at once, and asking far too few
Working too slowly on small tasks, and too quickly on large ones
Faking depth you lack, and demanding depth a call never needed
items.explanation: Both come from treating the choice as an accident instead of a decision.

items.prompt: Priya has never touched mobile power management and has until morning. What is the third option besides faking it or refusing?
choices: Find the owner, ask a sharp question, then check the answer
Approve quickly and watch for complaints afterwards
Ask the VP to decide, since the VP made the request
items.explanation: The third option is borrowed judgment from the real owner, checked.

items.prompt: Which factor asks how much damage a wrong call does?
choices: Reversibility
Stakes
Surface area
items.explanation: Stakes measures the damage from a wrong call.

items.prompt: Which factor asks how cheaply a wrong call can be undone?
choices: Reversibility
Time-to-signal
Stakes
items.explanation: Reversibility is the cost of undoing a wrong call.

items.prompt: Which factor asks how fast a wrong call shows itself?
choices: Stakes
Time-to-signal
Failure-mode coverage
items.explanation: Time-to-signal is how soon a mistake surfaces on its own.

items.prompt: When is breadth alone enough?
choices: When the domain belongs to another team entirely and they have said so
When the deadline is shorter than a day
When stakes, reversibility and time-to-signal are all low
items.explanation: Breadth is enough only when all three factors are low.

items.prompt: How many of the three factors need to be high for a call to earn real care?
choices: All three at once
Any one of them
At least two of them
items.explanation: Any single high factor is enough, because borrowed judgment is risky there.

items.prompt: Priya's battery drain would appear slowly, in reviews and tickets over weeks. Which factor is that?
choices: A failure that is easy to undo
A low-stakes call
Slow time-to-signal
items.explanation: A failure that surfaces slowly has a slow time-to-signal.

items.prompt: A wording change to an internal tool's error message is reverted in seconds and noticed at once. How does it read?
choices: Low on all three, so breadth is enough
High on stakes, so depth is warranted
Slow to show, so wait and watch for weeks
items.explanation: Internal, trivially undone and instantly visible: low on every factor.

items.prompt: A doctor can recheck a mild cough next week at no cost. What does that do to the factors?
choices: It raises the stakes, which raises the need for depth
It makes the signal slower, which raises the need for depth
It makes the call easy to undo, which lowers the need for depth
items.explanation: A free recheck means high reversibility, so less personal depth is needed.

items.prompt: Who is the right person to ask?
choices: Whoever has depth in the specific mechanism
Whoever replies first in the team chat
The highest-ranking person who happens to be available
items.explanation: The owner of the mechanism has depth; speed and rank do not show it.

items.prompt: Which question is the sharpest?
choices: Is this safe to ship?
Does a 15-minute interval hold the radio awake long enough to matter?
Could you take a look and tell me whether this seems fine to you overall?
items.explanation: It names a mechanism and a threshold, so the answer is checkable.

items.prompt: What does a sharp question let the expert do?
choices: Give a specific answer you can check
Skip the explanation and give only a verdict
Answer without thinking about the context
items.explanation: Specificity produces an answer you can test.

items.prompt: After an expert answers, what should you do next?
choices: Act on it at once, since they are the owner
Ask for the reasoning and check it
Ask a second expert only if you disliked it
items.explanation: An expert's answer is better informed, not yet verified.

items.prompt: Which answer signals a checkable explanation?
choices: It is delivered quickly, calmly and with confidence
It comes with several reassuring phrases
It names a mechanism that could turn out wrong
items.explanation: A named mechanism can be tested; fluency cannot.

items.prompt: Which reply does 'is this safe?' tend to get?
choices: A detailed answer covering every risk involved
A vague, hedged reply
A refusal to answer the question at all
items.explanation: Without a defined dimension, the honest reply is vague.

items.prompt: A sharp question is most closely related to which earlier unit's skill?
choices: Spaced repetition: reviewing material at widening gaps over time
Note-taking: capturing ideas
Weighing credibility: specific claims are easier to check
items.explanation: Specificity is the credibility signal, applied to a live conversation.

items.prompt: An answer from a real expert is...
choices: Better informed than a guess, but not yet verified
Verified, because experts are rarely wrong in their own field
Worthless, since experts can always be wrong
items.explanation: Experts raise your odds; checking still matters.

items.prompt: Whom did Priya ask first?
choices: The engineer who wrote the sync scheduler
The VP who had requested the review
The mobile team's manager
items.explanation: She went to the quickest and most available person first.

items.prompt: What was wrong with Priya's first question?
choices: It asked for a verdict and named no mechanism
It was too long for a chat message
It was sent after the deadline had passed
items.explanation: 'Any battery concerns?' asked for a verdict, so nothing could be checked.

items.prompt: What did Deja's answer rely on?
choices: A test run against the new interval before release
A memory of past changes, not of this one
Telemetry from the release
items.explanation: She recalled earlier changes, not this specific one.

items.prompt: Was Deja dishonest?
choices: No: the person and the question were not sharp enough
Yes, she knew the change was unsafe
Yes, she deliberately hid that no battery test existed for it
items.explanation: She answered in good faith; the gap was in the setup.

items.prompt: What tipped Priya off before she sent the approval?
choices: Marcus contradicted Deja in a team meeting
She could not say in one sentence why it was safe
The test suite turned red at 5:45pm on the release branch
items.explanation: The inability to explain why is the tell.

items.prompt: Who pointed Priya to the person who wrote the scheduler?
choices: The VP
A test report
Deja
items.explanation: Deja knew who owned the code and named Marcus.

items.prompt: Why were green tests not enough?
choices: Green tests are unreliable on mobile code in general, so they prove very little
Tests cover what authors expected, not unthought-of battery drain
Tests only run on the final release build
items.explanation: Tests check expected behavior, not failures nobody thought of.

items.prompt: Why is a quick, friendly answer risky?
choices: Friendly people are usually wrong about code
Quick answers always come from the wrong team
It feels trustworthy without being checkable
items.explanation: Tone and speed add comfort, not evidence.

items.prompt: What did Priya tell the VP to do?
choices: Ship to 1% and watch battery telemetry for 48 hours
Ship to everyone and monitor reviews afterwards
Block the change until automated battery tests exist
items.explanation: She chose a canary sized to the slow, costly failure.

items.prompt: Why a canary?
choices: It proves the change is safe for all users
It removes the need to ask an expert
It makes a slow failure fast to see
items.explanation: A canary shortens detection time for a slow-surfacing problem.

items.prompt: Why did Priya ask how Marcus knew past canaries worked?
choices: To get a track record, not just a claim
To test whether Marcus was in a good mood
To hand the VP a longer written report
items.explanation: Two real incidents made the answer defensible.

items.prompt: What did Marcus say about testing before release?
choices: CI catches battery drain within an hour of each commit being merged
No automated battery test exists, so testing will not catch it
Only manual tests run by the VP would catch it
items.explanation: The gap was no battery test, so the canary was the mitigation.

items.prompt: Why did Priya neither approve nor block?
choices: A sized mitigation fit what she learned
She wanted to avoid taking any responsibility
The VP had asked her to stay neutral
items.explanation: Approval would ignore the gap; blocking would ignore the mitigation.

items.prompt: If drain complaints appear after the canary anyway, what follows?
choices: Asking an expert was wrong, so go deep next time
It was still a sound bet with cheap detection
Experts should be ignored on mobile calls
items.explanation: Even good answers are not guarantees; fast detection limits the damage.

items.prompt: If the change were a config flag flippable in minutes, what shifts?
choices: Stakes vanish, so no one needs to check anything
Time-to-signal gets slower, so more care is needed
Reversibility rises, so a canary may be overkill
items.explanation: Higher reversibility lowers the need for a heavy mitigation.

items.prompt: What does the harm chart show, using an assumed $40 per day?
choices: Surfacing in 2 days costs 840, against 80 for 21 days
Surfacing in 2 days costs 80, against 840 for 21 days
The cost is the same whenever the problem surfaces
items.explanation: 2 x 40 = 80 and 21 x 40 = 840; faster detection means less harm.

items.prompt: Pat is asked to approve a change in a system they have never used, and replies 'sounds like a connection pool issue' because the term sounds plausible. What went wrong?
choices: Pat relied on breadth, which is never acceptable for unfamiliar systems
Pat faked depth, using borrowed vocabulary with no judgment behind it
Pat borrowed judgment, but from the wrong kind of expert
Pat over-investigated, spending effort the call never needed
items.explanation: Pat used a plausible term as a guess, which is the bluffing mode. Breadth would have meant admitting the limit and asking the owner.
items.reference:
Breadth, depth and the two ways to get it wrong
🩺 Breadth: knows the limits and who to call
🔬 Depth: can verify the claim alone
🎭 Faking depth, or 🔍 demanding depth the call never needed
Why: breadth is the default, depth is earned by a specific call, and borrowed judgment still needs a check.
items.learnMore:
Breadth versus depth is a decision, not an accident

Nobody can go deep on every domain a broad role touches, so breadth is the sensible default. Depth is the exception that a specific decision has to earn.

Common mistake

Treating shallow knowledge as a failure, which pushes people toward bluffing or toward wasting days.
items.reflection: Think of a field outside your own where you rely on someone else's judgment. How do you decide when to trust it and when to check?

items.prompt: A manager blocks three days to master a subsystem, to settle a trivial, easily undone question that a short chat with its owner would have answered. What is the diagnosis?
choices: Demanding depth that the call had not earned
Healthy diligence, since more depth is always safer
Bluffing, because the manager avoided asking anyone
Borrowed judgment applied without any check at all
items.explanation: Three days on a low-stakes, reversible question is the over-investigating mode, not diligence.

choices: Breadth is for easy calls only; borrowed judgment is for hard calls only

Breadth means asking nobody at all; borrowed judgment means asking everybody involved
Breadth is what you know; borrowed judgment is acting on an owner's reasoning
items.explanation: Breadth is your own working familiarity. Borrowed judgment is a separate act: using someone else's reasoning, checked.

Over-investigation limited by a single phone call

items.prompt: A migration changes customer billing data, cannot be undone once run, and any error would show in invoices the same day. Which reading is right?
choices: Low on all three, because errors show up the same day
High stakes and hard to undo, so depth is warranted
Breadth is enough, since a fast signal removes the risk
Only time-to-signal matters here, so the call is low risk
items.explanation: Two factors are high, and a fast signal does not cancel them. Fast detection helps after harm starts, not before.
items.reference:
Three questions about any call
💥 Stakes: how much damage if wrong?
↩️ Reversibility: how cheaply undone?
⏱️ Time-to-signal: how fast does it show?
Why: a call is safe on breadth only when all three are low; any one being high earns care.
items.learnMore:
Read all three factors together

Stakes, reversibility and time-to-signal each catch a different way a mistake becomes expensive. A quiet failure can matter even when stakes look modest.

Common mistake

Judging a call by stakes alone and ignoring that a failure nobody sees keeps growing.
items.reflection: Pick a decision you made recently in an area you did not know well. Which of the three factors was highest, and did you treat it that way?

Do the study, since hidden irreversible risk is probably there
Refuse to review until the framework's owner has approved

items.reference:
Three moves with an expert
🔎 Find the owner of the mechanism
❓ Ask a question sharp enough to check
✅ Check the reasoning before acting
Why: a vague question or the wrong person gives a confident answer you cannot test.
